clinicalPearls: An autosomal recessive organic aciduria of leucine catabolism caused by mutations in MCCC1 or MCCC2, which encode the subunits of the biotin-dependent enzyme 3-methylcrotonyl-CoA carboxylase.
It is one of the most frequently detected disorders on expanded newborn screening, flagged by a raised hydroxy-C5 (3-hydroxyisovaleryl) acylcarnitine.
The phenotype is highly variable: the majority remain asymptomatic, while a minority have episodic metabolic decompensation.
Crises are typically precipitated by fasting or intercurrent illness, with vomiting, lethargy, hypoglycaemia, metabolic acidosis and hyperammonaemia.
Urine organic acids show 3-hydroxyisovaleric acid and 3-methylcrotonylglycine, and secondary carnitine deficiency is common.
A positive newborn screen may actually reflect an affected, often asymptomatic, mother rather than the infant.
Unlike holocarboxylase synthetase and biotinidase deficiency, it is not biotin-responsive because the apoenzyme itself is defective.
Management rests on avoiding prolonged fasting, a written emergency sick-day regimen and carnitine supplementation, with mild leucine restriction reserved for symptomatic individuals.
reference.pathophysiology: 3-Methylcrotonyl-CoA carboxylase is a mitochondrial biotin-dependent enzyme that catalyses the carboxylation of 3-methylcrotonyl-CoA to 3-methylglutaconyl-CoA, the fourth step in the degradation of the branched-chain amino acid leucine. Loss-of-function mutations in the alpha subunit (MCCC1) or beta subunit (MCCC2) block this step, so 3-methylcrotonyl-CoA accumulates and is diverted to 3-methylcrotonylglycine and 3-hydroxyisovaleric acid, which are excreted in the urine. Conjugation of these intermediates depletes free carnitine and produces a secondary carnitine deficiency. The accumulated metabolites and impaired energy yield from leucine become clinically important mainly during catabolic stress, when they can precipitate hypoglycaemia, metabolic acidosis and encephalopathy, although many individuals never decompensate.
additionalDifferentials: Isovaleric acidaemia and other branched-chain organic acidaemias
Multiple carboxylase deficiency (holocarboxylase synthetase and biotinidase deficiency)
Maternal 3-methylcrotonyl-CoA carboxylase deficiency detected through the infant's screen
Medium-chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase deficiency and other fatty-acid oxidation defects
additionalInvestigations: Blood ammonia, glucose and acid-base status during acute illness
Molecular genetic testing of MCCC1 and MCCC2, with maternal testing when the infant screen is positive
redFlags: Acute encephalopathy or reduced conscious level during intercurrent illness
Persistent vomiting and poor feeding threatening a catabolic state
reference.prognosis: The outlook is generally good, with most individuals remaining asymptomatic and developing normally; rare severe presentations occur, but with avoidance of catabolism and prompt treatment of metabolic crises the prognosis is usually favourable.
pitfalls: Assuming a positive newborn screen always means the infant is affected, when it may reflect maternal disease
Giving biotin in the expectation of a therapeutic response
Failing to provide a written emergency regimen for illness
Imposing unnecessary protein restriction on an asymptomatic child
references: Inborn errors of metabolism references (standard reference)
management: Avoidance of prolonged fasting with prompt provision of carbohydrate to prevent catabolic decompensation, as most affected individuals remain asymptomatic.
Emergency sick-day regimen during illness or perioperatively using generous glucose-based feeds or intravenous dextrose.
Carnitine supplementation to correct the common secondary carnitine deficiency.
Moderate dietary leucine or protein restriction reserved for those with recurrent symptoms or biochemical disturbance, guided by a metabolic dietitian.
Treatment of acute crises directed at hypoglycaemia, metabolic acidosis and hyperammonaemia.
Monitoring of growth, development and carnitine status.
Genetic counselling for this autosomal recessive disorder, with maternal testing when a newborn screen is positive since an asymptomatic mother may be the source.
